title: Continuous Integration and Delivery on Linux
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of Continuous Integration and Delivery on Linux and identify key concepts from the supplied syllabus.
Use an appropriate read-only check or controlled example to demonstrate continuous integration and delivery on linux.
Describe one common failure mode, safety consideration, or platform/version difference relevant to this topic.

content.intro: This lesson introduces continuous integration and delivery on linux as part of production operations, cloud, and reliability. Begin with an observation you can safely repeat, then explain what the result tells you and what it does not prove.
content.why_it_matters: Operate cloud-hosted Linux workloads with reproducible provisioning, release strategies, monitoring, backup, and recovery.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Operational reliability depends on declarative changes, staged releases, observability, verified backups, and demonstrated recovery—not a deployment command alone.

items.title: Build agents
items.text: Build agents: Use the tool appropriate to the distribution, inspect proposed changes first, and note the package/runtime version that determines behavior.

items.title: Automated tests
items.text: Automated tests: Identify the concept’s role in the workflow, choose a read-only inspection first, and record the version or distribution details that could change the result.

items.title: Deployment scripts
items.text: Deployment scripts: Try a small reproducible command with quoted inputs, inspect standard output and error separately, and check the exit status as well as the printed text.

items.title: Artifact handling
items.text: Artifact handling: Identify the concept’s role in the workflow, choose a read-only inspection first, and record the version or distribution details that could change the result.

items.title: Rollback and release verification
items.text: Rollback and release verification: A backup or rollback is useful only when its integrity and restoration procedure have been verified in a separate test location.

content_blocks.execution_mode: manual-terminal; requires a local Linux environment or disposable VM; no isolated Linux runner is provided by CodeLeaf
content_blocks.expected_output: Whitespace/error checks for the current Git diff; outside a repository Git reports an error.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Use a Linux machine, WSL environment, or disposable virtual machine. Check the command with its local manual page before adapting it. The in-page example shows reference output only; it does not execute Bash/Linux commands on the CodeLeaf server. Commands and output formats may vary by distribution and installed utility version.
content_blocks.reset_steps: These example commands are read-only or print-only. Exit the terminal when finished; if you adapt the task to create files, use a disposable practice folder and remove only the test files you deliberately created.
content_blocks.example_review_note: Topic-specific draft example authored for Linux course. Output is environment-dependent where stated; review on the target distribution before publishing.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: First, state what you expect from the example. Run it in the intended environment, capture standard output and any error message, and inspect the exit status where meaningful. Then connect the observation to this lesson: Continuous Integration and Delivery on Linux. Do not infer more than the evidence supports.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake
content_blocks.text: A common mistake is to assume continuous integration and delivery on linux behaves identically on every distribution, kernel, utility version, and administrative policy. Verify the installed tool and consult the matching manual before using the procedure elsewhere.

content_blocks.title: Safety and compatibility
content_blocks.text: A successful deployment is not evidence of a working backup until restoration is tested. For commands that edit files, manage services, change network/firewall state, partition disks, change permissions recursively, or alter boot settings, use an isolated VM, take a snapshot/backup, review the exact target, and prepare a recovery path before acting.

content_blocks.title: Troubleshooting and reset
content_blocks.text: If the command is missing, check whether the required package is installed and which distribution you are using. If access is denied, do not immediately escalate to root; confirm the target path, identity, and required permission. If the result differs, capture the command, output, version, and environment so the issue can be reproduced.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: Remember the core relationship: Operational reliability depends on declarative changes, staged releases, observability, verified backups, and demonstrated recovery—not a deployment command alone. The goal is to explain the observed result, test a boundary case, and record a limitation rather than memorize a command in isolation.

content.task: In an isolated Linux lab, investigate continuous integration and delivery on linux. Use the guided example as a starting point, record the output/status, and test one boundary, failure, or distribution-specific case. Explain what you learned without changing a production system.
task_acceptance_criteria: The practical step is aligned to this lesson and uses synthetic inputs or a disposable environment.
The submission records expected and observed behavior, including an exit status or error when relevant.
One boundary case, failure path, or version/distribution difference is tested and explained.
Any potentially destructive command is previewed and kept out of production; the result can be reproduced.
hints: Start with read-only inspection and use the manual page for the installed command.
Change one variable at a time and preserve the exact output/error.
Record the distribution, kernel/utility version, privileges, and any assumptions that affect the result.
recap: Operational reliability depends on declarative changes, staged releases, observability, verified backups, and demonstrated recovery—not a deployment command alone.
Use evidence rather than assumptions; make platform differences explicit.
Protect credentials and data, and plan how to reverse state-changing operations.
